lessons.title: Schema design, session hygiene and plugin management
lessons.eli5: A schema is a form with labelled boxes, so every answer lands in the right place. Session hygiene is wiping the whiteboard before a new meeting, so old scribbles don't get mistaken for notes. Plugins are ready-made toolboxes you bolt onto Claude's coding assistant — only install ones you trust, because each takes up desk space even when you're not using it.
lessons.body:
## Schema design

Schemas show up in three places in a Claude app: **tool `input_schema`**, **structured output formats** (`output_config.format`, or `strict: true` on a tool), and **your own API contracts** that consume Claude's output. Good schemas make Claude's job easier and your parsing safer.

Principles:

| Principle | Why | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Clear, specific names | Claude reads names as meaning | `invoice_total_usd` beats `val1` |
| Descriptions on fields and tools | They are instructions; they steer selection and filling | "ISO 8601 date the invoice was issued; null if not printed" |
| `enum` for closed sets | Prevents creative variants | `"priority": {"enum": ["low", "normal", "urgent"]}` |
| `required` only when the data always exists | Forcing a value the source lacks invites invention | Make `po_number` nullable instead of required |
| An escape hatch | Lets Claude say "none of these" honestly | Add `"other"` plus an `other_detail` string |
| Flat over deeply nested | Easier to fill and validate | Avoid nesting four levels for a simple record |
| Separate tools for different risks | Lets you gate them differently | `get_order` (read) vs `refund_order` (write, approval) |

```json
{
  "name": "log_support_ticket",
  "description": "Record a classified support ticket. Use once per customer email after reading it fully.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "bug", "how_to", "account", "other"]},
      "category_detail": {"type": ["string", "null"], "description": "Detail when category is 'other'; null otherwise"},
      "customer_id": {"type": ["string", "null"], "description": "Exactly as written in the email; null if absent"},
      "urgency": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "normal", "urgent"]}
    },
    "required": ["category", "urgency", "customer_id", "category_detail"]
  }
}
```

Remember: **strict schemas guarantee format, not truth.** Values can still be wrong (and enum casing isn't guaranteed), so validate semantics in code (does the customer exist? do line items sum to the total?). Version schemas like APIs: adding an optional field is compatible; renaming or removing a field is a breaking change for consumers.

## Session hygiene

Context is a budget, and old context is not neutral: stale or irrelevant material dilutes attention and can steer answers ("context rot"). Hygiene keeps each session focused.

### In Claude Code
- **One task per session.** Use `/clear` when switching to unrelated work; it starts a fresh conversation (the old one can be resumed later).
- **`/compact [focus]`** summarises the conversation in place when you want to continue the same task with less context. Summaries lose detail, so keep exact facts (IDs, numbers, decisions) in files such as a plan or notes file.
- **`/context`** shows what is using the window, including which memory files loaded.
- **Delegate noisy exploration to subagents** so search output stays out of the main session.
- **Resume deliberately** (`--continue`, `--resume`) only when the earlier context is still relevant; otherwise start fresh with a short written handoff.
- **Rewind** (`/rewind`, or Esc Esc) to back out of a wrong path instead of arguing with it in the same context. Checkpoints don't track file changes made by shell commands, so git remains the safety net for those.

### In API applications
You own the history, so hygiene is your code's job:
- Keep only what the next turn needs; trim or summarise old turns.
- Prune large tool results once they've been used, or use server-side context editing and compaction where appropriate.
- Persist durable facts (user profile, decisions) in your database and inject them as a compact block, rather than relying on a sprawling transcript.
- Never let one user's session data leak into another's: session state is keyed per user and per conversation.

## Plugin management (Claude Code)

A **plugin** bundles skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and output styles under one name, described by a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest. Plugins come from **marketplaces** (catalogues such as a git repository with a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`); browse and manage them with `/plugin`.

Practices:
- **Install deliberately and review first.** Plugins run code as you, with your permissions (hooks, MCP servers). Review what a plugin bundles before trusting it, and prefer approved internal marketplaces. You can load a plugin straight from a folder with `--plugin-dir <path>` when testing your own.
- **Scope correctly.** Install at user scope for personal tools, project scope (recorded in the committed `.claude/settings.json`) for tools the whole team should use, local scope for personal per-project experiments.
- **Keep the set lean.** Every enabled plugin's skill and agent descriptions consume context. Disable what you don't use (`claude plugin disable`, or through `/plugin`).
- **Update on purpose.** Treat plugin versions and plugin dependencies as supply-chain decisions: pin what you have tested and re-review when something changes (see Configuration management).
- **Organisation control.** Administrators can use managed settings to allowlist or block marketplaces and to force-install required plugins.

## Worked example

A platform team ships a `payments-dev` plugin with a deploy skill, a code-review agent and an MCP server for the internal ledger API. They publish it in an internal marketplace, enable it via project scope in the payments repo, disable two legacy plugins nobody was using, and ask engineers to `/clear` between unrelated tickets because long mixed sessions were producing reviews that referenced the wrong service.
keyTakeaways: Schemas are instructions: clear names, field descriptions, enums for closed sets, nullable fields for data that may be absent.
Strict schemas guarantee shape, not correctness; validate semantics in code and version schemas like APIs.
Session hygiene: one task per session, /clear between unrelated tasks, /compact to continue with less context, durable facts in files.
In API apps you own history: trim, prune tool output, persist facts outside the transcript, isolate sessions per user.
Plugins bundle executable components; review before installing, scope correctly, keep the set lean, and pin tested dependency versions.
examTips: If extraction invents values for missing data, the fix is a nullable or optional field plus validation, not a stricter 'required'.
Answers that start a fresh session (with a concise handoff) usually beat continuing a long, drifting session.
For team-wide plugins, choose project scope committed to the repo, not each person's user scope.
Treat plugin installation as a supply-chain decision: review, approved marketplace, pinned versions.
commonTraps: Making every field required, which pushes the model to fabricate values.
Assuming /compact keeps exact numbers and IDs intact.
Enabling many unused plugins, which costs context on every turn.
Installing a plugin from an unknown marketplace without reviewing its hooks or MCP servers.

lessons.title: Configuration management: CLAUDE.md, settings, model pinning, prompt and plugin versions
lessons.eli5: Configuration is the recipe card taped inside the kitchen cupboard. If everyone cooks from the same card, kept in one place and updated carefully, the food tastes the same every day. If people scribble private changes, swap ingredients without telling anyone, or the supplier quietly changes the flour, the food changes and nobody knows why.
lessons.body:
## What needs configuration management

A Claude system's behaviour depends on more than code: instruction files, settings, the model version, prompt text and installed plugins. Configuration management means each of these is **versioned, reviewed, reproducible and deliberately changed**. The CCDV-F blueprint names exactly these components for this skill: CLAUDE.md files, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning, and plugin dependencies.

## CLAUDE.md: the instruction hierarchy

| Scope | Location | Shared with |
|---|---|---|
| Managed (organisation) | IT-deployed system path (`/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` on Linux/WSL, `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` on macOS, `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md` on Windows) | Whole organisation; cannot be excluded by individual settings |
| User | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Only you, all projects |
| Project | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` | The team, via git |
| Local | `./CLAUDE.local.md` (gitignored) | Only you, this project |
| Subdirectory | `some/dir/CLAUDE.md` | Loaded on demand when Claude reads files there |

Key behaviours: files are **concatenated, not overridden** (broad first, more specific later); `@path` imports organise content but still load at launch (recursive imports stop at 4 hops); `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` globs load only when matching files are read; keep each file concise (the docs suggest under about 200 lines). CLAUDE.md is guidance delivered as context, not enforcement — anything that must always happen needs a hook or a permission rule.

Team rule: anything every contributor needs goes in the **project** file in git. A classic failure is putting team conventions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, where new teammates never see them.

## settings.json: scopes and precedence

| Scope | File |
|---|---|
| Managed | `managed-settings.json` in the system paths above (or server-managed settings from the claude.ai console) |
| Command line | flags such as `--settings`, `--model`, `--permission-mode` |
| Local | `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal, gitignored) |
| Project | `.claude/settings.json` (committed) |
| User | `~/.claude/settings.json` |

**Precedence, highest first: managed > command line > local > project > user.** Scalar keys at a higher level override lower ones; list-valued keys such as `permissions.allow` **merge** across levels. Don't over-generalise "managed always wins": a few restrictive keys (for example `maxEffortLevel`) honour a stricter value from a lower scope. Settings hold permissions (allow/ask/deny), hooks, the default model and more. Shared enforcement (deny rules, hooks) belongs in project or managed settings — managed hooks cannot be disabled from lower scopes; personal tweaks in local or user settings.

## Model version pinning

Anthropic ships model generations over time (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and so on), and the exam blueprint explicitly calls out **breaking behaviour changes across model releases**. Pinning means the model string in your configuration is an explicit, reviewed choice.

On the Claude API you request a specific model ID such as `claude-opus-5-5` or `claude-haiku-4-5`. Newer generations can also reject parameters older ones accepted: a prefilled assistant message returns HTTP 400 on Claude 4.6 and later, forced `tool_choice` (`any`/`tool`) returns 400 on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, and manual extended thinking is rejected on Claude 4.7 and later. A model change is a code-adjacent change, not a drop-in swap.

In Claude Code the model can be an alias (`opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku`) or a full model ID, set in settings, agent frontmatter or `--model`. An alias is shorthand, not an exact version identifier — use the full ID when reproducibility matters. Environment variables interact with the setting: `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` overrides the settings `model` key, while `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` applies only when no settings file sets `model`.

Production practice:
- Pin an exact model ID in config, not scattered through code.
- Treat a model change as a **release**: run the eval suite on old vs new, review prompt adjustments (new generations change behaviour and may reject parameters your code sends), roll out gradually, keep a rollback path.
- Track model releases and plan migrations instead of discovering them in production.

## Prompt versioning

Prompts are code. Manage them the same way:
- Store prompts as files in the repository (or a prompt registry) with an identifier and version.
- Change them through pull requests; record why the change was made.
- **Tie each version to eval results.** A prompt change merges only if evals hold or improve.
- **Log the prompt version and model ID with every request,** so a production regression can be traced to the change that caused it.
- Roll back by redeploying the previous version, not by hand-editing production.

## Plugin dependencies

A plugin installs as a unit — skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers together — described by a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest and distributed through a marketplace (a repo with a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`). Plugins install at user, project or local scope; project installs are recorded in committed `.claude/settings.json` (each collaborator still installs it), and managed settings can allowlist or block marketplaces and force-install plugins.

Two facts to manage: every enabled plugin's skill and agent descriptions occupy context **every turn**, and plugins run code on your machine. Treat a plugin like any other dependency: review what an update changes, keep the installed set deliberate, and prune what you don't use.

## Secrets are not configuration you commit

Keep keys and tokens out of CLAUDE.md, settings files and `.mcp.json`. Use environment variables (`.mcp.json` supports `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` expansion in command, args, env, url and headers, keeping secrets out of git), CI secrets (GitHub Secrets for workflows) and a secrets manager.

## Worked example

After a quiet update, a team's Claude Code review bot starts flagging style issues it used to ignore. Investigation: the model setting had been bumped to a newer generation without re-running evals — and had the pipeline relied on assistant prefill or forced `tool_choice`, it would have failed outright with 400s — plus a teammate had edited the review prompt in place on the CI server. Fixes: pin the exact model ID in the workflow; move the prompt into the repo with a version tag; add a CI eval that replays 50 historical PRs and compares findings; put the shared deny rules in committed project settings. The next model upgrade becomes a reviewed PR with eval results attached.
keyTakeaways: CLAUDE.md files concatenate broad-to-specific (managed, user, project, local; subdirectories lazy-load); team conventions belong in the project file in git.
settings.json precedence: managed > CLI flags > local > project > user; list-valued keys like permissions.allow merge across files (a few restrictive keys excepted).
Pin exact model IDs when reproducibility matters; in Claude Code ANTHROPIC_MODEL overrides the model setting and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL applies only when no settings file sets model.
Version prompts in source control, gate changes on evals, and log prompt version plus model ID per request.
Plugins bundle skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers as one unit, cost context every turn and run code — review plugin changes like any other dependency.
examTips: Behaviour changed with no code change? Suspect an unpinned model generation, an unversioned prompt edit or an unreviewed settings/plugin change.
A teammate missing instructions means they were put in user-level CLAUDE.md; move them to the project file.
Precedence runs managed > CLI > local > project > user, but list keys merge rather than replace — and a few restrictive keys let stricter lower-scope values win.
Treat model upgrades as releases: compare evals old vs new, expect parameter-level breakage on newer generations (prefill, forced tool_choice, manual thinking), keep a rollback path.
commonTraps: Thinking a more specific CLAUDE.md replaces broader ones; they are concatenated.
Relying on an alias (sonnet, opus, haiku) instead of a full model ID when you need reproducible behaviour.
Editing prompts directly in production with no version history.
Letting plugins update unreviewed; they change skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers together and run code on your machine.
Committing secrets in .mcp.json or settings instead of using ${VAR} references and secret stores.

lessons.title: Applications and Integration drill (one-third of the exam)
lessons.eli5: This is the practice lap before the real race. Each short story hides one clue that gives away the right answer — like a doctor who hears a single symptom and instantly knows the illness.
lessons.body:
## How this domain is tested

Applications and Integration is about **a third of the Developer exam**, roughly 17 to 18 of 53 items. The six skills, by weight: Claude Application Design (8.6%), Software Engineering Foundations (7.4%), Claude API Mechanics (6.8%), Configuration Management (4.1%), Understanding Requirements (3.4%), Systems Life Cycle (2.8%). Expect general engineering questions with no Claude feature in them alongside API-specific ones.

## A four-step method

1. **Name the binding constraint.** Who is waiting? What volume? What sensitivity? What must always happen?
2. **Name the layer.** Requirements, lifecycle stage, API mechanic, engineering practice, instruction surface, or configuration?
3. **Eliminate options that solve a different problem** (more power when cost is the issue, prompts when enforcement is needed, retries for client errors).
4. **Prefer the root-cause fix with the least machinery.**

## Practice situations

Try each before reading the reasoning.

**1. Weekly compliance digest.** Every Sunday, 40,000 short policy exceptions are summarised for a Monday report. Cost matters.
Reasoning: nobody waits, volume is high, so use the **Message Batches API**; match by `custom_id`; add a 1-hour cache on the shared instructions. Parallel sync calls don't lower price.

**2. Chat feels frozen.** Users of an internal assistant see a blank screen for eight seconds, then the full answer.
Reasoning: perceived latency. **Stream** the response. Raising `max_tokens` doesn't address it, and a batch job would make it far worse.

**3. Truncated JSON in a stream.** A tool's arguments occasionally fail to parse while streaming.
Reasoning: the code parses `input_json_delta` chunks early. Accumulate and parse after **`content_block_stop`**.

**4. Retry storm.** A service retries every failed Claude call immediately, five times. Logs show 400 errors and 429s.
Reasoning: don't retry 400s (fix the request); for 429 honour `retry-after` with exponential backoff and bounded concurrency. The SDK already retries 429 and 5xx.

**5. Duplicate refunds.** After timeouts, a worker re-sent `POST /refunds` and some customers were refunded twice.
Reasoning: POST isn't idempotent. Use an **idempotency key** or check state before retrying.

**6. New hire gets no conventions.** Senior engineers' Claude Code sessions follow the team's test conventions, but a new hire's don't.
Reasoning: the conventions live in each senior's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Move them to the **project `CLAUDE.md`** in git.

**7. Silent behaviour change.** A CI review bot's output changed over a weekend with no repo commits.
Reasoning: the job uses the `sonnet` alias in Claude Code, which now points at a newer model. **Pin a full model ID** and treat upgrades as releases with evals.

**8. Injected instructions.** A research assistant that reads supplier websites tried to email a contact list after visiting one page.
Reasoning: keep web content as untrusted data in tool results, state that in the system prompt, and make the email tool **approval-gated or unavailable**. A polite instruction alone isn't a control.

**9. Invented purchase-order numbers.** An extraction schema marks `po_number` as required; documents without one come back with plausible fake numbers.
Reasoning: make the field **nullable**, instruct to return null when absent, and validate against the source.

**10. Same file, many calls.** A web app asks dozens of questions about the same 150-page PDF per user session.
Reasoning: send the PDF as a **document block at the top of each request** with a `cache_control` breakpoint after it, and put the question after; repeat questions then read the cache at a tenth of the base input price. For very large files there is the Files API (500 MB request limit).

**11. Requirements gap.** A team built a beautiful agent for invoice approval, then learned finance requires every approval above a threshold to be signed off by a person and logged.
Reasoning: a non-functional requirement (auditability, human approval) was missed. Add a **deterministic approval gate and audit log**; capture such constraints during requirements next time.

**12. Big migration.** Claude Code must move 300 files from one ORM to another.
Reasoning: **plan mode** first, characterisation tests, migrate module by module on branches, run tests at each step, independent review.

**13. Drifting session.** After four hours on unrelated tickets in one Claude Code session, suggestions start referencing the wrong service.
Reasoning: session hygiene. **`/clear`** between unrelated tasks, keep durable notes in files, use subagents for exploration.

**14. Plugin update broke the deploy skill.** A shared plugin's dependency released a major version that renamed an MCP tool.
Reasoning: declare the dependency with a **constrained version range**, test against it, and widen the range only deliberately, after re-testing.

**15. Cloud choice.** A bank requires all AI calls to go through its existing AWS accounts and IAM.
Reasoning: **Amazon Bedrock**; then verify that every feature the design relies on is actually available there (for example, fast mode runs on the first-party API only, and not with Batch).

**16. Model retirement.** Your app is pinned to an older model with an announced retirement date next quarter.
Reasoning: lifecycle maintenance. Run the eval suite on the successor now, adjust prompts and parameters, stage the rollout before the date.

## Last-minute checklist

- Required request fields: `model`, `max_tokens`, `messages`; `system` is top-level.
- Stateless API: resend history; your app owns session state.
- Batch: 50% off, up to 24 h, 100,000 requests / 256 MB, `custom_id`, 29-day results, no streaming.
- Streaming: SSE; mid-stream errors after 200; parse tool JSON at `content_block_stop`.
- Thinking: adaptive plus `output_config.effort` on current models; billed as output; counts toward `max_tokens`.
- 4xx fix, 429 wait, 5xx/529 back off; POST isn't idempotent.
- Settings precedence: managed > CLI > local > project > user; lists merge. CLAUDE.md concatenates.
- Pin models, version prompts, constrain plugin dependencies, keep secrets out of config.
keyTakeaways: Find the binding constraint first; most D2 answers follow from who is waiting, volume, sensitivity or 'must always'.
Batches for latency-tolerant bulk work, streaming for humans watching, cached document blocks for reused files.
Don't retry client errors; honour retry-after on 429; make retried writes idempotent.
Team conventions in project CLAUDE.md; pin model IDs; version prompts; constrain plugin dependency versions.
Untrusted content is data, and enforcement (approval gates, least privilege) backs every content boundary.
examTips: About one in three exam items comes from this domain; budget review time accordingly.
Several options may work; choose the one that fixes the root cause with the least added machinery.
Eliminate options that change an unrelated variable (temperature, model size, max_tokens) when the problem is architectural.
General software-engineering questions are in scope; don't over-think them into Claude features.
commonTraps: Reaching for a bigger model when the scenario's real constraint is cost, latency or enforcement.
Treating prompts as enforcement for behaviours that must always happen.
Forgetting that the batch API can take up to 24 hours.
Confusing Claude Code aliases (which move) with Claude API model IDs (pinned snapshots).
